title: What to Serve with Pesto Chicken: Sides That Let the Basil Lead
description: What to serve with pesto chicken: starchy sides that soak up the sauce, vegetables that match basil's sweetness, and portion amounts for the full plate.
imageAlt: Bowl of trofie pasta with pesto, green beans, potato chunks, and fresh basil leaves.
photoCredit: Eluinie, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
keywords: what to serve with pesto chicken
summary: Pesto chicken already brings fat, salt, and herbal sweetness — the sides job is texture and starchy support. These pairings follow the Ligurian rule: pesto loves potatoes, green beans, and anything that absorbs rather than competes.
quickWins: Starches that absorb sauce beat crisp sides: boiled potatoes, gnocchi, rice, and soft polenta are pesto's traditional partners.
Green vegetables with natural sweetness — green beans, asparagus, zucchini — echo basil instead of fighting it.
Keep added dairy mild: pesto carries parmesan already, so sour cream or extra cheese crowds it.
Brighten the finish with lemon or cherry tomatoes; pesto's olive-oil richness flattens without one fresh note.

sections.heading: What pesto needs from a side dish
body: Pesto is a dense, oily, salty condiment: basil, garlic, parmesan, pine nuts, and olive oil. Chicken carries it well because the meat is neutral and tender, but the rest of the plate has to solve two problems — soak up the oil so it does not pool, and add texture the soft chicken and silky sauce cannot provide.

Liguria, pesto's home region, answered both questions with one plate: trofie pasta with boiled potato chunks and green beans tossed straight into the pot with the pasta. The potatoes absorb the oil, the beans add snap, and the pasta carries the sauce. That template — starch plus green vegetable plus pesto — is the backbone of every pairing below.
sections.callout: The Ligurian test: a good pesto-chicken side either absorbs the sauce or adds crunch. Fries, onion rings, and garlic bread do neither — they add more oil and more salt.

sections.heading: Starches that soak up the sauce
body: Pesto clings to ridged and twisted shapes and pools beside flat ones. Boiled potatoes are the traditional choice and the best absorber of all.

sections.heading: Vegetables that match basil's sweetness
body: Basil is sweet, peppery, and anise-like. The vegetables that pair best share the warm-weather garden profile or bring snap and bitterness for contrast.
bullets: Green beans — blanched then tossed with a spoon of the pesto; the direct link to the classic plate (3 oz).
Blistered cherry tomatoes — their acid lifts the oil (1 cup for two people).
Grilled zucchini ribbons — smoky, soft, and neutral (4 oz).
Asparagus — charred tips add bitterness that offsets the parmesan salt (4–5 spears).
Arugula salad — peppery leaves, lemon, shaved parmesan; no croutons needed (2 oz).
Roasted broccolini — slightly bitter, sweet stems; a drizzle of the same pesto ties it in.

sections.heading: Sauces and accents beyond extra pesto
body: Pesto is already the sauce, so additions should be small accents that change the plate's temperature or acidity rather than new sauces entirely.
bullets: Lemon wedges — non-negotiable; a squeeze at the table wakes up both chicken and potatoes.
Balsamic drizzle — on the tomato or arugula side only, not the pesto itself.
Chili crisp or Calabrian chili paste — a 1/2 tsp for heat lovers; basil and chili are old partners.
Toasted pine nuts or walnuts — sprinkle for crunch; the pesto's nuts are usually blended smooth.
Whipped ricotta — a mild, creamy counterpoint if the pesto tastes too sharp or salty.

sections.heading: The Ligurian one-pot method
body: The fastest complete version of this plate comes straight from Genoa: boil potatoes and green beans in the same pot as the pasta. Waxy potato chunks go in first (8 minutes), green beans and pasta follow for the final minutes, and everything drains together, still wet enough to melt a spoonful of pesto into a light sauce. Sliced pesto chicken goes on top; the pasta underneath catches what falls.

Cooking times at a glance: baby potatoes 12–15 minutes, green beans 4–5 minutes, trofie or fusilli 9–11 minutes — all in one pot, staged. The residual starch on the pasta emulsifies the pesto, which is why the sauce clings without cream.

sections.heading: Wine-safe and leftover notes
body: For guests who want a glass with dinner, crisp whites are the safe pour: Vermentino (Liguria's own), Pinot Grigio, or a dry Sauvignon Blanc — high-acid wines that refresh the palate against the oil. Heavy oak Chardonnay stacks woody notes on nutty pesto and flattens both.

Leftover pesto chicken turns into tomorrow's lunch easily: shred it over the remaining starch with a spoon of pasta water or a squeeze of lemon to loosen the sauce. Pesto darkens in the fridge but stays safe for 3–4 days in a sealed container; keep a thin layer of olive oil on top of open pesto to slow oxidation.
bullets: Store pesto separately from cut chicken; combine only at serving.
Freeze extra pesto in ice-cube trays; thaw exactly the cubes you need.
Cold leftover trofie pesto salad: add cherry tomatoes and arugula, serve straight from the fridge.
Reheat chicken gently (steamer or 300°F oven); microwave at full power makes the pesto oil split.
